quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken continuously?
quests.hint: A cluster ends the first word. Say it quickly. What survives at the end?
quests.explanation: In quick speech the final /t/ of 'next' is light, so what you hear connecting is the /s/ moving into 'on'. Queues and agendas use this phrase constantly.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken as one smooth unit?
quests.hint: Quiz time. What is the final sound of the adjective, and what begins the next word?
quests.explanation: Reading a list, you would say 'last' and 'answer' separately. In real speech the /s/ (and /t/ if pronounced) runs into the opening vowel of 'answer'.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which pair blends so tightly it could be heard as a name?
quests.hint: Which pair blends so tightly it could be heard as a name?
quests.explanation: This one fools people into hearing a name. 'Just in' is heard as 'Justin' because the final consonant of 'just' flows into the vowel of 'in', which shows how completely a link can blend two words.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which two words run together?
quests.hint: A sound spelled 'th' ends the first word. What happens when a vowel follows?
quests.explanation: The breathy /θ/ at the end of 'worth' continues straight into the weak /ə/ of 'a'. A gap there would turn easy encouragement into something much heavier.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Find the natural transition
quests.hint: People's names count. Look for the one that starts with a vowel.
quests.explanation: Names are not exempt. 'With' ends in /ð/ (or /θ/ in some accents), and the airflow carries on into the /æ/ of 'Anna'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that blends into one chunk
quests.hint: A date. The ordinal ends with a breathy 'th'.
quests.explanation: Dates are said quickly. The /θ/ of 'fourth' slides into the weak /əv/, and then 'of July' cannot link, because /v/ meets /dʒ/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Spot the linking point
quests.hint: Think of the verb ending spelled 's' that sounds like a buzz.
quests.explanation: The verb ending is a /z/, and you keep your voice on it as you move into the weak /ə/ at the start of 'alone'. Turning it into a /s/ would sound off.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Say it aloud: which words join up?
quests.hint: A job-related verb ends in a syllable that sounds like 'iz'.
quests.explanation: Job talk: 'teaches' ends in /ɪz/ and 'English' starts with another /ɪ/, so the last /z/ is the bridge. 'Brother teaches' does not link, because 'teaches' starts with /t/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which pair would a fluent speaker say in one breath?
quests.hint: Plural nouns end in a buzzing sound. Which one is followed by a weak vowel?
quests.explanation: Plural nouns end in a buzz, and 'are' is weak, /ə/. So the /z/ of 'buses' lands on it. 'Are late' offers no link at all.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Skip the tempting boundary and find the real link
quests.hint: The first two words might look linked. Check the first sound of the second one.
quests.explanation: 'Get back' looks as if it could link, but /t/ meets /b/. The real link is the next one: the /k/ of 'back' goes straight into the vowel of 'in'.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which boundary has no pause?
quests.hint: A place word meets a short connector. What does the place word end with?
quests.explanation: 'Home' ends in /m/, so your lips are closed when 'and' begins, and the weak /ən/ rolls out of the hum. 'Came home' cannot link because 'home' starts with /h/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which words melt together when you say this naturally?
quests.hint: The particle here is part of the verb. What does the verb end with?
quests.explanation: 'Up' is part of the verb here, so it belongs to 'look': the /k/ goes directly into /ʌ/. 'Up the' cannot link: /p/ + /ð/.
quests.flowRule: Phrasal verbs: In a verb plus particle (log in, fill out, look up), the particle usually starts with a vowel, so the two words are spoken as one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: Listen for the connected words
quests.hint: Choice questions at the till link the alternatives. What is the very small word in the middle?
quests.explanation: 'Or' is usually just /ə/ in a choice question, and /ʃ/ flows into it easily, so 'cash or card' is heard as one smooth chunk.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Identify the linked pair
quests.hint: 'This week' does not link. Why not?
quests.explanation: 'This week' looks tempting, but /s/ meets /w/. The /k/ of 'week' is the one that links, into the weak 'or'.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Read the line aloud and join the right pair
quests.hint: The question offers two options. Which boundary goes into the little word between them?
quests.explanation: 'Good or bad' is a three-beat chunk, and linking is why: the /d/ is released into 'or', so the two options are heard as a pair.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken as one smooth unit?
quests.hint: A quick acknowledgement. Which word links into the final word?
quests.explanation: People say 'got it' as one word. The /t/ is released straight onto /ɪ/, so the whole phrase lasts barely longer than 'got' on its own.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which pair would sound choppy if you stopped between them?
quests.hint: A short future contraction runs into the verb after it.
quests.explanation: 'I'll' contains the /l/ that links, and 'ask' has an open vowel start, so the pair runs on. 'Ask Sam' cannot link, since /k/ meets /s/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Tap the pair that sounds like one word
quests.hint: Wishing someone well. What does the noun end with?
quests.explanation: Wishes are said quickly and warmly. The /k/ of 'luck' lands on 'on'. 'Good luck' has /d/ + /l/ and does not link.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Find the natural transition
quests.hint: Technology trouble. Which past-tense verb runs into the last word?
quests.explanation: Technology complaints often end with 'again'. The /t/ of 'crashed' goes into the weak /ə/ at the start of 'again'. 'Website crashed' does not link, because /t/ meets /k/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Find the pair that blends into one chunk
quests.hint: A software complaint. Which verb ends with a sound that can run into the next word?
quests.explanation: The /s/ after /p/ ends 'keeps', and it flows into the opening vowel of 'asking'. 'Asking me' offers /ŋ/ + /m/, so no vowel there.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Find the smooth connection
quests.hint: Advice from IT support. Find the verb followed by a short pronoun.
quests.explanation: 'It' is weak and attaches to the verb before it: the /d/ of 'download' flows into it. 'Should download' cannot link, because /d/ meets /d/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Say it aloud: which words join up?
quests.hint: A teacher's request. Which word before 'aloud' ends in a consonant?
quests.explanation: A teacher says 'read aloud' as one unit. 'Aloud' begins with /ə/, so the /d/ of 'read' fills the gap. 'Can you' cannot link: /n/ + /j/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which pair would a fluent speaker say in one breath?
quests.hint: Classroom instruction. A very common verb meets a very weak word.
quests.explanation: 'At' is weak, so the /k/ of 'look' glides onto it. 'At page' then goes /t/ + /p/, with no vowel.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which pair is spoken continuously?
quests.hint: Two small words sit side by side. Which pair connects?
quests.explanation: Two small words side by side: the /z/ of 'has' lands on the /ə/ of 'a'. 'Who has' has no link, because /h/ is a consonant.
quests.flowRule: Weak Function Words: Short grammar words such as a, an, of, at, and, or and it are normally unstressed and begin with a vowel sound, so they attach to the word before them.

quests.instruction: Which boundary has no pause?
quests.hint: A family visit. Which noun ends in a cluster before a verb that starts with a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Parents' ends in a cluster, and the /s/ at the end is what links, into the weak /ə/ at the start of 'arrive'. 'Jack's parents' cannot link, since /s/ meets /p/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which words melt together when you say this naturally?
quests.hint: Housework. Find the verb followed by a particle.
quests.explanation: Housework talk. 'Clean' ends in /n/ and 'up' starts with a vowel, so they flow together. 'Help me' offers /p/ + /m/, so no link there.
quests.flowRule: Phrasal verbs: In a verb plus particle (log in, fill out, look up), the particle usually starts with a vowel, so the two words are spoken as one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: Which two words run together?
quests.hint: Someone's pet has been naughty. Which noun ends in a voiced stop before a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Dog' ends in /g/ and 'ate' begins with /eɪ/, so the /g/ links into it. 'Ate my' does not link, because /t/ meets /m/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Identify the linked pair
quests.hint: Making plans with a friend. Which verb ends in 'ch' before a vowel?
quests.explanation: Friends say this loosely and fast. The 'ch' of 'catch' flows into 'up'. 'Up soon' cannot link: /p/ + /s/.
quests.flowRule: Phrasal verbs: In a verb plus particle (log in, fill out, look up), the particle usually starts with a vowel, so the two words are spoken as one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: Read the line aloud and join the right pair
quests.hint: A text you might send. Which -ing word runs into a weak vowel?
quests.explanation: A late text, read aloud, would run as one phrase. The /ŋ/ bridges into the weak /ə/, and 'a bit' and 'bit late' each have a consonant on one side.
quests.flowRule: Linking after -ing: The -ing ending is the single nasal /ŋ/. It stays voiced and flows into a following vowel, with no pause and no added /g/.

quests.instruction: Spot the linking point
quests.hint: A presenter opens a meeting. Which pair does not pause?
quests.explanation: A presenter opening a meeting wants to sound warm and confident. The /ŋ/ of 'morning' flows into the vowel of 'everyone', and then 'everyone welcome' does not link (/n/ + /w/).
quests.flowRule: Linking after -ing: The -ing ending is the single nasal /ŋ/. It stays voiced and flows into a following vowel, with no pause and no added /g/.
